subtype: Approach: quitting after the first difficult stage [Pitfall]
passage: On the fifth day of flute practice, Akash's lips ached and every second note squeaked like a rubber toy. He lowered the flute. "I'm not made for this," he told his sister Irawati, who was doing homework at the same table. "Everyone at class plays properly. I just hiss." He wiped the flute, laid it in its case and shut the latch. The next evening he watched cartoons instead. The evening after that, he did not even glance at the shelf. The case stayed shut.

qa.q: What happened to the notes when Akash played?
What was Akash feeling when he lowered the flute?
qa.a: Discouraged, since he believed he was not made for the flute.

qa.q: What could Akash do instead of quitting, and why?
qa.a: He could ask his teacher whether squeaks are common at the start and keep to short sessions, so the sore lips have time to settle.

qa.q: How might Irawati see Akash's decision to stop?
qa.a: Irawati sees him give up quickly and may want to encourage him, although she says nothing.

grounding: A boy stops flute practice when his lips hurt and the notes squeak, feeling he has no talent.

subtype: Approach: quitting after the first difficult stage [Pitfall]
passage:
"Pradeep, where's your flute? Class is starting."
"At home. In the cupboard. I'm stopping, Tenzin."
"Stopping? It's been two weeks!"
"My lips hurt after five minutes. And every note squeaks like a door. You heard it."
"Everyone squeaks. I squeaked for a month."
"Your squeaks sounded better than mine."
"They sounded exactly the same, trust me."
"No. Some people just have talent. I don't."
"Sir said the first few weeks are the worst."
"Sir says that to everyone."
The music teacher began the scale, and eleven flutes piped up. Pradeep sat with his empty hands under the desk. By the end of term Tenzin could play the whole school song.

qa.q: How long had Pradeep been learning the flute?
What does Pradeep believe about himself, and how does he feel?
qa.a: He believes he has no talent, and he feels discouraged and embarrassed by the squeaks.

qa.q: What else could Pradeep have tried?
qa.a: Shorter practice sessions and asking the teacher about his lip position, to get through the sore, squeaky stage.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see Pradeep quitting?
qa.a: Tenzin is surprised and tries to encourage him, insisting his own squeaks sounded the same.

grounding: A boy quits the flute when his lips hurt and the notes squeak, believing he lacks talent, while his friend keeps going.

subtype: Approach: quitting after the first difficult stage [Pitfall]
passage: When I was nine, I, Bhupen, took up the bamboo flute because my cousin Kiran was learning. For the first ten days my lips went sore and numb, and every note came out as a hiss or a shriek. Kiran's notes sounded clear to me. I decided I just didn't have it, and I put the flute in the drawer under my bed. Nobody told me, and I didn't ask, that almost everyone sounds like a kettle at first. Years later Kiran told me the teacher had said it to the whole class: the first month hurts. I had missed that class. Kiran plays at weddings now. My flute is still in the drawer, and sometimes I take it out and wonder.

qa.q: Where did Bhupen put the flute?
qa.a: In the drawer under the bed.

qa.q: How does Bhupen feel now when taking the flute out?
qa.a: Wistful and a little regretful, wondering what might have been.

qa.q: What else could Bhupen have done in those first ten days?
qa.a: Ask Kiran or the teacher whether sore lips and squeaks are normal, and keep going with short practices.

qa.q: What was the first month like for Kiran?
qa.a: Kiran heard the teacher say the first month hurts, kept going through it, and now plays at weddings.

grounding: Looking back, a child describes quitting the flute during the painful beginner stage without knowing most learners go through it.
